html:
An API is a promise: once clients depend on it, every change can break someone. These ten rules keep APIs predictable for the people who call them, and leave you room to change them later.

1. Name Resources With Plural Nouns

URLs name things; HTTP methods say what to do with them.

GET    /orders          list orders
POST   /orders          create an order
GET    /orders/42       read order 42
PATCH  /orders/42       change part of order 42
DELETE /orders/42       delete order 42

Avoid verbs in paths like /getOrders or /createOrder. Nest only to show ownership, and only one level deep: /customers/7/orders is clear, /customers/7/orders/42/items/3/notes is not.

2. Use the Methods for What They Mean

Method Use Safe Idempotent
GET Read Yes Yes
POST Create, or run an action No No
PUT Replace a whole resource No Yes
PATCH Change some fields No Not necessarily
DELETE Remove No Yes

Safe means it changes nothing; idempotent means doing it twice has the same effect as once. A GET must never change data: crawlers, prefetching and caches call it freely.

For actions that don't fit, like cancelling an order, a sub-resource reads well: POST /orders/42/cancellation.

3. Return Honest Status Codes

Clients and monitoring tools rely on them. The ones you need most:

  • 200 OK, 201 Created (with a Location header), 204 No Content.
  • 400 Bad Request for malformed input, 422 Unprocessable Content for valid JSON that breaks rules.
  • 401 Unauthorized when not logged in, 403 Forbidden when logged in but not allowed.
  • 404 Not Found, 409 Conflict for a state clash, like a duplicate email.
  • 429 Too Many Requests, with Retry-After.
  • 500 for your bugs, 503 when temporarily down.

Never answer 200 with {"error": "..."} in the body: every client then has to read the body to know whether it worked. The HTTP status codes reference explains each one.

4. Use One Error Format Everywhere

Pick a shape and use it for every error, so clients write the handling once:

{
  "type": "validation_error",
  "message": "Some fields are invalid.",
  "errors": [
    { "field": "email", "message": "Must be a valid email address." },
    { "field": "quantity", "message": "Must be at least 1." }
  ],
  "requestId": "req_8f2a"
}

A stable type lets code react; message is for people; a requestId lets support find the logs. The standard RFC 9457 "problem details" format is a good starting point.

5. Paginate Every List

A list that's small today grows. Return pages from day one:

GET /orders?limit=50&cursor=eyJpZCI6MTA0fQ
{
  "data": [ ... ],
  "nextCursor": "eyJpZCI6MTU0fQ"
}

Cursor pagination (start after the last item seen) stays fast on huge tables and doesn't skip or repeat items when new rows arrive. Offset pagination (?page=3) is simpler and allows jumping to a page, but slows down deep into large tables. Cap limit, so no one asks for a million rows.

6. Filter, Sort and Select With Query Parameters

GET /orders?status=paid&created_after=2026-01-01&sort=-created_at&fields=id,total

Use the same names across the whole API. A minus sign for descending order and a fields parameter for smaller responses are common conventions.

7. Make Retries Safe With Idempotency Keys

Networks fail, and clients retry. Retrying a POST /payments after a timeout must not charge twice. Let clients send a key:

POST /payments
Idempotency-Key: 6c1a2e9b-3f4d-4a7e-9a51-0e2c8b7d4f10

The server stores the result under that key and returns the same response for a repeat, without doing the work again. It matters for anything that creates or moves something valuable.

8. Version From the Start

Breaking changes will come. Put a version in the path, /v1/orders, or in a header. Then:

  • Additive changes, like a new optional field or a new endpoint, don't need a new version.
  • Breaking changes, like removing or renaming a field or changing its type, do.
  • Announce deprecations early and give clients months to move.

Clients should ignore fields they don't know, so you can add fields freely.

9. Be Consistent in the Small Things

Inconsistency costs clients more than any single choice:

  • One naming style for JSON fields: camelCase or snake_case, not both.
  • Dates in ISO 8601 with a time zone: 2026-11-21T09:30:00Z.
  • Money as an integer in the smallest unit, plus a currency: {"amount": 1999, "currency": "EUR"}. Floats round badly.
  • IDs as strings, so they can change format later.

10. Secure and Document It

  • HTTPS only, with authentication on every endpoint except the ones meant to be public.
  • Check permissions per resource: being logged in doesn't mean you may read order 42.
  • Rate limit, and validate every input.
  • Publish an OpenAPI description, with examples of real requests and responses. If an example is hard to write, the endpoint is probably hard to use.

The Rules in Short

  1. Plural nouns for resources, methods for actions.
  2. Methods with their real meaning; GET never changes data.
  3. Honest status codes, never 200 with an error.
  4. One error format, with a type, a message and a request ID.
  5. Paginate every list, preferably with cursors.
  6. Filtering, sorting and fields through query parameters.
  7. Idempotency keys for anything that mustn't happen twice.
  8. A version from day one; additive changes don't need a new one.
  9. Consistent names, dates, money and IDs.
  10. HTTPS, permissions per resource, rate limits and real documentation.
